newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood renews Taleban ultimatum as Afghans battle.
newsitem.headline: Masood renews Taleban ultimatum as Afghans battle.

text.p: Ousted government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood told Taleban fighters on Friday to quit the Afghan capital as newfound allies in his battle against the Islamic militia came under heavy fire.
Forces loyal to Uzbek General Abdul Rashid Dostum were hammered by Taleban mortars on Friday, less than 24 hours after joining Masood's front line north of Kabul, witnesses said.
A senior Uzbek officer said Dostum's men would join Masood's forces in an offensive later in the day and Masood issued his second ultimatum in three days to the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban.

"We want the Taleban to evacuate Kabul," Masood told Reuters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj north of the front line. "A limited international force under U.N. supervision should control Kabul and pave the way for all-party talks on a broad-based government."
Heavy tank, rocket and artillery fire was being traded between Taleban and ousted government forces, but Masood insisted neither side had yet launched a full assault.

"It is only an exchange of artillery on both sides," he told reporters on Friday at his base in Jabal os-Siraj. "The Taleban are trying to hold Bagram airbase and to strengthen their forces at the (Bagram) road junction. That is it."
Masood, who won fame as a guerrilla leader for his exploits against Soviet troops in the 1980s, made clear the alternative was war.
As he spoke, mortar bombs and rockets from his forces rained down on positions around the key Bagram junction north of Kabul held by the Taleban, who drove Masood from Kabul three weeks ago.
Fighting was still going on in the late afternoon, despite a heavy rainstorm that drenched plains north of the capital.

The Uzbeks, descendants of the Mongols of Genghis Khan, were hit hard by mortar bombs that fell on their positions at the rate of one a minute at times south of Charikar, a 30-minute drive from Jabal os-Siraj.
They sought shelter behind natural and man-made fortifications in the foothills west of the main highway.
In Rabat, the local Dostum commander said he had sustained four casualties since joining the front line on Thursday afternoon and was expecting an order to attack in retaliation some time on Friday.

"We are together now, Jumbush and Jamiat, and we are going to attack the Taleban because they have been attacking us," Gholam Sahky, commander of Dostum's 88th division, told reporters as rounds fell with 50 metres of his position.

Dostum sent a dozen tanks and several hundred men to join Masood on Thursday after formally recognising the government driven from Kabul and promising to back Masood if the Taleban did not stop fighting.
Dostum's Jumbush troops and Masood's Jamiat soldiers have been enemies more often than not since the mujahideen came to power in Kabul in 1992.
The Uzbeks held talks with Taleban leaders on Wednesday and Thursday, but there was no word on any outcome beyond a Taleban spokesman saying he was hopeful an understanding could be reached.
More talks were scheduled for Friday, but Sahky told reporters the Uzbeks and Masood's men would attack.

"We are going to have a strong attack against the (Bagram) junction and when the attack is over we will control that junction," he said. "We expect reinforcements and then the order to attack some time later today."

Masood insisted the Taleban quit Kabul. "If the Taleban are not ready to cooperate with us, we cannot avoid fighting," Masood said in Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush which his men retook in a counter-attack a week ago.

A Taleban evacuation of Kabul was floated at the United Nations. The United States called it "probably premature", although State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said a proposal to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea".
There was no immediate reaction from the Taleban on Friday, the Islamic day of rest, but they had rejected the earlier Masood ultimatum and vowed to defend Kabul.
